strengths: Novel application of semiparametric efficient estimation theory to LLM evaluation with rigorous theoretical framework
Solid asymptotic theory: Theorem 4.1 establishes √N-consistency and semiparametric efficiency bound under practical assumptions that are weaker than standard results
Well-controlled simulation study validates theoretical predictions and confirms tracking of Oracle EIF estimate
Comprehensive real-world experiments across three benchmarks (GPQA Diamond, AIME 2025, GSM8K) with 10 models and two auxiliary configurations
Clear problem motivation: demonstrates real reproducibility crisis in LLM evaluation with compelling concrete example
Pragmatic adaptations for practice: semantic regression approach for small-sample regimes (N=30) is creative
General framework: extends beyond pairwise comparisons to arbitrary auxiliary signals sharing information with target outcome
weaknesses: Empirical improvements are often modest and lack statistical significance testing: Table 1 mostly <2%, Table 3 often <1%; no confidence intervals or hypothesis tests provided to validate significance
Some models show negative improvement (Table 2: Qwen3 -1.06% to -5.33%, Llama -1.66%) suggesting method isn't universally beneficial; conditions for when gains are realized are underexplored

Critical design choices lack justification: (1) why M=500 for simulations but M=10 for real experiments with no sensitivity analysis; (2) K=5 folds chosen without ablation; (3) subset sizes (N=50, N=15, N=100) unexplained

Assumption 3.1 treating p(z|x) as 'known' because accessible via Monte Carlo sampling requires careful interpretation; gap between classical notion of known distributions and sampling-based approximation underexplored

Nuisance function estimation for small samples uses frozen LLM (Gemini-3-Flash) as semantic regressor without ablation studies or theoretical justification; risks of systematic bias propagation not addressed
Computational costs completely absent: requires generating M+1 auxiliary responses and pairwise comparisons per instance; no wall-clock time, API cost, or overhead analysis provided

Semantic regression approach (Remark 3.3) relegated to brief remark despite being critical for small-sample regime; limited justification for why pre-trained LLM reasoning transfers to nuisance estimation task
Limited analysis of when/why large efficiency gains occur in practice; no characterization of required correlation structure between auxiliary and primary outcomes needed for substantial improvements
No direct empirical comparison against cited related work (Frick et al. 2025, Zhou et al. 2025) using same data/models despite claiming advances over their control variate approaches

strengths: Addresses a genuine problem in LLM evaluation: high variance estimates and unstable model rankings due to small benchmark sizes and model stochasticity
Sound theoretical framework grounded in semiparametric efficiency theory; Theorem 4.5 and Corollary 4.7 are rigorously proven with reasonable assumptions
Well-motivated use of generation-verification gap: pairwise comparisons are shown to be more stable than absolute correctness judgments
Comprehensive experimental validation across three benchmarks (GPQA, AIME, GSM8K) with 10 diverse models and extensive robustness checks
Practical algorithms provided for both standard regression (Algorithm 1) and small-sample semantic regression (Algorithm 2) settings
Honest limitations discussion acknowledging finite-sample degradation when auxiliary signals are weak
General framework extending beyond pairwise comparisons to arbitrary auxiliary signals and other metrics
weaknesses: Practical improvements are modest (1-5% in most cases) and inconsistent; many configurations show negative or near-zero gains (e.g., Table 2), raising questions about real-world significance despite theoretical elegance
No computational cost analysis; generating M auxiliary responses per instance requires ~10× more model calls, but cost-benefit tradeoff is never discussed
Ground truth in real experiments is defined as naive estimator on full dataset—itself a noisy estimate, not ground truth—undermining empirical validation of theoretical claims about efficiency gains
Success depends critically on τ̂ quality, but auxiliary signal quality assessment is left to practitioners with no guidance; Figure 5 shows sharp degradation with auxiliary noise
Semantic regression approach (Algorithm 2) using LLM as fixed regressor for τ(x,z) lacks theoretical justification; why should general-purpose LLM estimate target model's correctness accurately?
Limited theoretical novelty: core contribution applies established semiparametric efficiency theory (Kennedy 2022; Robins et al.) to new domain; EIF derivation follows standard techniques
Asymptotic theory (N → ∞) but small samples (AIME: N=30); no finite-sample analysis, concentration bounds, or practical validity assessment of asymptotic guarantees in finite-sample regimes
Missing key comparisons: no evaluation against Bayesian approaches, limited comparison to repeated-Y baseline (4/5 models improved), absent comparison to related variance reduction methods
Limited experimental scope: only accuracy metric tested; only mathematical reasoning domain; extension to pass@k deferred as future work
Inconsistent design choices: token limits differ between target (32,768) and auxiliary responses (8,192-2,048); justification in Remark C.1 is ad-hoc, not principled
No confidence intervals, significance tests, or statistical validation of reported improvements; gains could be within estimation noise

strengths: Addresses important reproducibility crisis in LLM evaluation with concrete examples of inconsistent reporting (e.g., 65.2% vs 40.2% accuracy on same model/benchmark)
Rigorous theoretical framework: correct EIF derivation, asymptotic normality (Theorem 4.5), and guaranteed strict variance reduction (Corollary 4.7)
Well-motivated key insight: leverages generation-verification gap—the observation that models can make reliable pairwise comparisons even when generation fails

Comprehensive experimental validation: controlled simulations with known ground truth, real-world experiments on three benchmarks, extensive robustness checks across auxiliary models/seeds/subset sizes/prompts
Practical algorithmic innovation: semantic regressor approach (Algorithm 2) elegantly handles small-sample problems (N=30 for AIME) without gradient-based fitting
Clear presentation with informative visualizations and transparent methodological choices; extensive appendices support reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: applies established EIF and one-step correction techniques (Robins et al. 1994, Kennedy 2022) to new domain rather than developing new statistical machinery

Circular validation on real data: ground truth defined as naive estimator on full dataset, which is precisely what the method aims to improve; true external validation on held-out human-verified labels would be stronger

Modest practical improvements: many results show 1-2 percentage point reductions (Tables 1-3), with some cases showing negative improvement (Table 2: QwQ-32B -1.66%, Qwen3-Next -5.33%); computational overhead not fully justified

Insufficient treatment of failure modes: Remark 5.1 acknowledges degradation when Z is weak but provides minimal guidance; missing analysis of when auxiliary judgments systematically disagree with ground truth
Computational overhead: requires M auxiliary samples (10 for real data, 500 for simulation) and pairwise comparison judgments; cost-benefit tradeoff insufficiently discussed for practitioners

Experimental design concerns: asymmetric token limits (32K target vs 8K auxiliary), semantic regressor fixed to Gemini-3-Flash without sensitivity analysis, limited robustness to weaker auxiliary models
Limited baseline comparisons: no comparison to recent variance reduction methods (Bayesian refinement, pairwise graphs), minimal exploration of repeated decoding alternative
Ranking accuracy conflation: simulation study emphasizes ranking accuracy, which conflates variance reduction with ordering recovery; direct point estimation comparisons would be clearer
Missing practical guidance: no clear decision framework for when practitioners should employ the method vs alternatives, insufficient sensitivity analysis to nuisance function quality
